title: Web crawler
summary: Crawl a billion pages a month politely: a host-partitioned frontier, layered dedup, robots.txt and a recrawl budget.
interviewerPrompt: Design a web crawler for a search engine. It starts from some seed URLs and keeps discovering and downloading pages so the index stays complete and fresh. Walk me through how you would build it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many pages do we need to fetch?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: About 1 billion pages a month, sustained, starting from a seed list operators provide.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How big is a typical page, and do we store it?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Assume 100 KB on average. Store the fetched content for the indexer, which consumes it separately.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are there limits on how hard we can hit a single site?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes: obey robots.txt and make at most one request per second to any single host, less if the site is slow or asks for less.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should we fetch the same URL more than once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Skip URLs we already have, and do not store pages that are near-duplicates of pages we already stored. Recrawls are planned, not accidental.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How fresh does the content need to be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Frequently changing pages should be recrawled more often than static ones, within a fixed fetch budget.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens when machines fail?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The crawl must keep making progress when machines fail; losing a few minutes of in-flight work is fine, losing the frontier is not.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we need to render JavaScript?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, fetch and parse HTML only. JavaScript rendering is out of scope.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Who uses the system directly?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: About 50 crawl operators who add seeds, watch progress and block or slow down hosts when site owners complain.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is latency of a single fetch important?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Throughput, politeness and freshness matter; nobody waits on an individual fetch.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we need to crawl from multiple regions?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not at first: one region with several availability zones. Discuss geographic fetching as a scaling step.

deepDiveQuestions: How do you design the URL frontier to enforce one request per second per host while keeping 400 fetches/s flowing?
How do you avoid fetching the same URL twice and storing near-duplicate pages?
How do you handle robots.txt and other politeness signals correctly?
How do you schedule recrawls so frequently changing pages stay fresh within a fixed fetch budget?
What happens when a fetcher or frontier machine dies mid-crawl?

requestTypes.name: URL-seen check for a discovered link
Fetch a page and store it

runChallenge.title: Keep crawling through a zone loss
runChallenge.description: At the 2× catch-up rate (800 fetches/s and 40,000 URL-seen checks/s), lose the availability zone holding the most components. The crawl must keep serving at least 40,000 operations/s with under 1% errors and no single point of failure.

commonMistakes: One global FIFO queue of URLs: consecutive links from the same site hammer one host or stall workers waiting for its politeness slot.
Partitioning the frontier by URL hash, which scatters a host across shards and turns per-host politeness into a distributed locking problem.
Never computing that discovery outruns fetching (about 5 new URLs found per page fetched), and so designing an unbounded, unprioritised frontier.
Using a Bloom filter without sizing it or stating what a false positive costs, or using one where a false positive is unacceptable (seeds, operator URLs).
Dedup by exact content hash only, which misses pages that differ just in timestamps, ads or session tokens.
Treating a robots.txt 5xx as permission to crawl, and ignoring 429 and 503 responses with Retry-After.
Assuming exactly-once fetching is achievable, instead of leases plus idempotent completion with harmless duplicate fetches.
Recrawling every page on the same schedule, or strictly in proportion to change rate, instead of spending a fixed budget where freshness gain per fetch is highest.
